executive_summary: Across 40 orders from January to October 2025, revenue is driven far more by which product is sold than by volume: unit price correlates with revenue at r = 0.78, versus r = 0.59 for units. Gizmo is the most-ordered product and the South the most active region. Discounts average 14.5% and about 22% of orders are returned, both worth investigating before scaling promotions.

key_findings.title: Price mix drives revenue more than volume
key_findings.detail: Revenue tracks unit price more closely than units sold, so shifting mix toward higher-priced products likely moves revenue more than pushing volume.

key_findings.title: Revenue per order is right-skewed
key_findings.detail: Mean revenue per order (685.06) sits well above the median (463.25), so a few large orders carry a disproportionate share.

key_findings.title: South leads order count
key_findings.detail: South accounts for the most orders among the four regions, followed by North.

key_findings.title: Returns are material
key_findings.detail: Roughly one in five orders is returned, a meaningful drag on realized revenue.

questions_answered.question: What drives revenue?
questions_answered.answer: Price mix, more than volume: unit price tracks revenue more closely than units.

open_questions.question: What margin does each product carry after discounts and returns?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Revenue alone may favor products that are less profitable.

open_questions.question: Why are two orders missing a region?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Gaps in regional attribution distort territory performance.

open_questions.question: Is there seasonality in weekly order value?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The data spans nine months, enough to check for early seasonal patterns.

hypotheses.statement: Shifting product mix toward Gizmo increases revenue per order.
hypotheses.rationale: Unit price has the strongest correlation with revenue in the profile.
hypotheses.test: A/B test merchandising that features Gizmo and compare revenue per order.

hypotheses.statement: Higher discounts do not increase units per order.
hypotheses.rationale: Discount shows no strong correlation with units (|r| < 0.5).
hypotheses.test: Regress units on discount, controlling for product and region.

hypotheses.rationale: The overall 22.5% return rate is high enough that it probably varies across segments.
hypotheses.test: Chi-square test of returned vs product.

recommended_actions: Join cost data to compute margin per product.
Break returns down by product and region.
Collect at least two more quarters of orders before setting pricing strategy.
data_quality_notes: discount is missing for 3 of 40 orders (7.5%).
region is missing for 2 of 40 orders (5%).
With only 40 orders, correlations are directional, not conclusive.

slides.title: What really drives our revenue
slides.subtitle: Nine months of orders show product mix matters more than volume

slides.headline: Revenue follows price mix, not order volume, and one in five orders comes back

takeaways.title: Price mix leads
takeaways.text: Unit price tracks revenue more closely than units sold, so shifting mix toward premium products moves the top line most.

takeaways.title: A few big orders
takeaways.text: Average order value sits well above the median: a handful of large orders carry a disproportionate share of revenue.

takeaways.title: Returns are material
takeaways.text: Roughly one in five orders is returned, a real drag on realized revenue that deserves its own investigation.

slides.title: Price, not volume, moves revenue
bullets: Unit price has the strongest relationship with revenue of any field.
Units sold matter, but noticeably less than which product is sold.
Discount shows no strong link to volume, so promotions may not pay.

slides.title: Gizmo leads a close product race
bullets: Gizmo is the most-ordered product, but the three are close.
Mix shifts toward Gizmo would lift revenue if its price holds.

slides.title: Order values are right-skewed
bullets: The median order is far below the largest, so outliers drive averages.
Report medians alongside means when tracking order value.

items.statement: Featuring Gizmo more prominently raises revenue per order.
items.test: A/B test merchandising that leads with Gizmo; compare revenue per order.

items.statement: Deeper discounts do not increase units per order.
items.test: Regress units on discount, controlling for product and region.

items.statement: Return rates differ meaningfully by product.
items.test: Chi-square test of returned versus product on the full order history.

slides.title: Recommended next steps
steps: Join cost data to compute margin per product before changing prices.
Break returns down by product and region to find the root cause.
Run the Gizmo merchandising test for four weeks.
Extend the analysis window to capture seasonality.
